changes.new: ### Toolformer: selecting data and deciding when to call The loss filter above operates after candidate calls have been proposed. It cannot retain a useful call that the generator never produced. In the published experiment, the default sampler first kept positions whose API-start probability exceeded 0.05, selected at most five such positions per document, and sampled up to five calls at each position. These are separate limits: five possible insertion sites can produce up to 25 candidates, not five final training examples. Calculator and translation examples were harder to obtain. Their recipe used a zero sampling threshold, up to 20 positions and ten candidates per position, with a lower loss-improvement threshold of 0.5 instead of 1.0. This increases the work spent proposing and executing candidates; it does not make every proposed call useful. The sampling and filtering settings are specified in [Toolformer, Supplement A](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/d842425e4bf79ba039352da0f658a906-Supplemental-Conference.pdf#page=1). For a small example, suppose API-start probabilities at six positions are 0.01, 0.08, 0.07, 0.04, 0.06 and 0.03. A threshold of 0.05 admits positions 1, 2 and 4 using zero-based indexing. A two-position budget retains 1 and 2. A high score at the third admitted position does not overcome that budget. The same idea applies to the published five-position limit. ~~~python def insertion_sites(probabilities, threshold, max_positions): eligible = [i for i, p in enumerate(probabilities) if p > threshold] return sorted(eligible, key=lambda i: (-probabilities[i], i))[:max_positions] p = [.01, .08, .07, .04, .06, .03] assert insertion_sites(p, .05, 2) == [1, 2] # A toy token ranking, not probabilities measured from GPT-J. def api_start_allowed(ranked_tokens, k, calls_already_made=0): return calls_already_made == 0 and "[API]" in ranked_tokens[:k] ranking = ["ordinary-word", "another-word", "[API]", "other"] assert not api_start_allowed(ranking, 1) assert api_start_allowed(ranking, 3) assert not api_start_allowed(ranking, 3, calls_already_made=1) ~~~ The stable index tie-break in this illustrative sampler makes its output reproducible; the paper does not specify it as an implementation requirement. The API marker in the second function is a toy vocabulary item. The original experiment uses existing token sequences rather than adding this literal token to GPT-J. The minimum in the filtering baseline has a separate purpose. Suppose loss is 3.0 with no call, 1.0 with the question alone, and 2.4 with the question and the result. Comparing only against 3.0 would report a gain of 0.6. Comparing against the required minimum, 1.0, gives −1.4, so the call is rejected. The generated question already helped the model more than the supplied answer did. This is why filtering against a single no-call baseline changes the method. #### The annotator sees more text than the deployed model The annotation prompt contains the document being annotated. It can use later text to propose an earlier call; ordinary inference cannot see that future continuation. Supplement A therefore removes translation examples whose translation input appears after the call but not before it. Otherwise the training sequence can teach the model to request a phrase that has not yet become available. Other tools also require source-specific preparation. The training calendar approximates a document's date from its URL and discards documents without an extractable date. It does not insert today's date into every historical paragraph. The calculator heuristics favor text containing arithmetic relations or several numbers. Atlas-large generates QA annotations, whereas Atlas-xxl answers QA calls at evaluation time. The language model's 6.7B parameters therefore do not describe the full system's inference cost. After execution and filtering, retained calls are inserted into the text. Multiple independently sampled calls can appear in an annotated document; the method does not build examples where a later tool consumes an earlier tool's result. The experiment also discards documents in which no call survived. Table 2 reports retained-call example counts under several thresholds, while Supplement B caps the training examples at 25,000 per API. Those counts are not all the same quantity. For instance, the QA, Wikipedia and calendar rows at threshold 1.0 contain 18,526, 60,974 and 20,587 examples before that cap; calculator and translation use threshold 0.5, with 3,680 and 3,156 examples. A large search row does not imply that all 60,974 search examples were used in the final capped recipe. Supplement B describes sequences of at most 1,024 tokens, effective batch size 128, up to 2,000 updates, and checkpoint selection on a separate CCNet development set. These are historical training settings, not budgets reproduced by the small examples here. #### Decoding changes the frequency of tool use The published zero-shot evaluation uses greedy decoding with a special exception: it starts an API call whenever the API-start marker is among the top ten candidates, even if another token ranks first. The toy ranking above illustrates the difference between a rank-one and rank-three trigger. This is an inference rule applied to the same weights. Supplement E reports that changing this rank limit from 1 to 10 raises the call rate on T-REx from 40.3% to 98.1%, and on WebQS from 8.5% to 100%. A high call rate is therefore not solely a learned preference of the model. The evaluation permits at most one call per input to prevent repeated calls. That cap is an experimental decoding constraint; it does not mean the augmented training documents contain at most one inserted call. When the model reaches the response delimiter, generation pauses. The executor supplies the real tool response and the closing delimiter, then the model resumes. A generated claim about what an API returned is not a substitute for that execution. Original Toolformer cannot use this loop to refine a search query repeatedly or compose several tools. #### What the reported measurements establish The paper evaluates language modeling with API calls disabled. GPT-J + CCNet and Toolformer-disabled both obtain perplexities 10.3 on WikiText and 10.5 on the held-out CCNet sample; the original GPT-J has 9.9 and 10.6. Thus the augmented run matches the unaugmented fine-tuning control in those two tests, while fine-tuning itself worsens WikiText relative to the original checkpoint. This does not prove preservation of every language capability. With calls enabled, evaluating a text's marginal probability would require accounting for possible calls; the reported comparison does not perform that calculation. The gain from a tool also depends on the model and the tool. In [Supplement G](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/d842425e4bf79ba039352da0f658a906-Supplemental-Conference.pdf#page=7), the stronger LLaMA v1 7B model benefits from the targeted Atlas QA tool on LAMA, but noisy BM25 search can hurt open-domain QA. The following rows use the appendix's QA evaluation prompt and answer-matching protocol: | LLaMA v1 7B condition | WebQS | Natural Questions | TriviaQA | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Original base model | 36.2 | 25.4 | 59.2 | | Self-generated Toolformer data, calls disabled | 37.0 | 27.6 | 60.2 | | Same fine-tuned model, calls enabled | 36.6 | 26.9 | 57.8 | The comparison between the last two rows isolates enabling calls for that fine-tuned checkpoint under the reported evaluation. It does not establish that search is generally harmful: the returned passages, call trigger, prompt and base knowledge all matter. The paper's scaling observation around 775M parameters is likewise specific to the tested GPT-2/GPT-J models and tools, with an exception for search; it is not a universal minimum model size for tool use. ### Где здесь MCP

### ReAct: prompting, fallback and learned trajectories A thought in the original ReAct formulation changes the text context available for the next decision. It does not move an object, run a search or supply an observation. This distinction is visible in the two examples above: naming Front Row prepares a search, and planning to open a drawer does not open it. The environment supplies the evidence after the action. The original prompts do not impose the same cadence on every task. For HotpotQA and FEVER, demonstrations contain a thought before each action. For ALFWorld and WebShop, thoughts occur at selected points: choosing a likely location, recognizing a completed subgoal, or revising the plan. Several actions can follow without another written thought. A rigid parser that requires one thought for every action would exclude some of these original decision-making trajectories. The HotpotQA prompt contains six annotated demonstrations; FEVER uses three. In ALFWorld, the authors annotate three demonstrations per task type and form six ordered two-example prompts. The model in the main prompting experiments is frozen PaLM-540B. These demonstrations provide examples of a policy; they are not gradient updates. #### Switching between retrieval and self-consistency ReAct can fail because search returns nothing useful or because its trajectory repeats a previous action. CoT can construct a useful reasoning sequence while relying on an incorrect remembered fact. Section 3.2 of [ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629v3) tests two ways to switch between the methods. In ReAct → CoT-SC, the controller first runs the environment-interaction trajectory. If it has not returned an answer within the chosen budget, it falls back to sampled CoT answers and voting. The original budgets are seven steps for HotpotQA and five for FEVER. Exhausting the budget is a controller event, not a model-generated proof that retrieval is impossible. In CoT-SC → ReAct, the controller samples several CoT answers first. If the most frequent answer appears fewer than half as many times as the number of samples, it invokes ReAct. With five samples and counts 2, 2 and 1, the test triggers retrieval; counts 3 and 2 do not. The rule uses answer agreement, not the probability that the answer is true. ~~~python from collections import Counter def fallback_to_react(extracted_answers): if not extracted_answers: raise ValueError("at least one sampled answer is required") largest_group = max(Counter(extracted_answers).values()) return largest_group < len(extracted_answers) / 2 assert fallback_to_react(["A", "A", "B", "B", "C"]) assert not fallback_to_react(["A", "A", "A", "B", "B"]) # The literal strict-inequality rule retains an exactly-half group. assert not fallback_to_react(["A", "A", "B", "B"]) # Agreement alone cannot detect five identical wrong answers. assert not fallback_to_react(["wrong"] * 5) ~~~ This example assumes answers have already been extracted and normalized. It does not infer equivalence between differently worded answers. The strict comparison is the heuristic stated in the paper; it is not a calibrated confidence test. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/agent-reconciliation-2026-10-30/react-cot-sampling.png]] *Shunyu Yao et al., [ReAct v3, Figure 2, PDF p. 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03629v3#page=5). CC BY 4.0. Complete original two-panel figure and English caption; surrounding paper text excluded.* The horizontal axis counts CoT-SC samples. It does not count all tokens, search requests or model invocations in a combined method. The two panels also use different metrics: exact match for HotpotQA and classification accuracy for FEVER. Their vertical values should not be averaged into one score. With the 21-sample CoT-SC baseline, Table 1 reports: | PaLM-540B prompting condition | HotpotQA EM | FEVER accuracy | |---|---:|---:| | CoT | 29.4 | 56.3 | | Act-only | 25.7 | 58.9 | | ReAct | 27.4 | 60.9 | | CoT-SC, 21 samples | 33.4 | 60.4 | | ReAct → CoT-SC | 35.1 | 62.0 | | CoT-SC → ReAct | 34.2 | 64.6 | ReAct beats Act-only on both tasks, but it does not beat CoT on HotpotQA in this comparison. The better combined condition differs between tasks. The curves support the authors' result that combinations can reach the 21-sample CoT-SC score with fewer CoT samples; they do not measure a corresponding fixed multiple of end-to-end cost savings. #### Reading the error analysis and the fine-tuning result Table 2 is a manually labeled analysis of 200 selected trajectories: successful and unsuccessful cases from both ReAct and CoT. The reported 0% hallucination category belongs to the selected ReAct failures. It is not a measured zero hallucination rate across every ReAct answer. The same table assigns 6% of selected ReAct successes to a false-positive category with hallucinated reasoning or facts: a correct final answer can coexist with a defective trajectory. Non-informative search, reasoning errors and answer-label ambiguity remain separate sources of failure. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/agent-reconciliation-2026-10-30/react-prompt-vs-finetune.png]] *Shunyu Yao et al., [ReAct v3, Figure 3, PDF p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03629v3#page=7). CC BY 4.0. Both original panels, legend, axes and English caption retained.* The left panel compares prompting formats at three PaLM sizes. ReAct performs poorly for the smaller prompted models, despite using the same reasoning-and-action format. The right panel uses 3,000 generated trajectories selected for correct final answers to fine-tune smaller models. The ranking changes: fine-tuned ReAct at 8B beats the tested 62B prompting conditions; fine-tuned ReAct at 62B beats the tested 540B prompting conditions. There is no 540B fine-tuning result in the right panel; its empty position must not be read as a zero score. This is task-specific evidence on HotpotQA, not a guarantee that a small fine-tuned agent beats every larger model. Selecting a correct final answer also does not certify every intermediate thought. At execution time, observations still come from the environment, even if training trajectories included observation text. The ALFWorld numbers use another experimental protocol. The often-quoted 71% is the best of six ReAct prompt choices on 134 unseen games; the mean over those choices is 57%. It should not replace the mean or be compared to a mean as if both used the same selection. WebShop evaluates 500 instructions and distinguishes attribute-coverage score from complete success; its reported ReAct success rate is 40.0%. These are the original benchmark conditions, not current leaderboard claims. ### Объём и полнота ответа
